title: Mercy Amid the Overthrow of Sodom
summary: Angels rescue Lot from wicked Sodom before the LORD destroys the cities by fire, yet Sodom’s influence follows Lot’s family into a mountain cave.
historicalContext: The cities of the plain lay in the low, well-watered region near the southern end of the Dead Sea, a district rich in bitumen and sulfurous deposits (14:10). Like other walled towns of the period, Sodom gathered its civic life at the gate, where elders sat, cases were heard, and strangers were observed. Hospitality to travelers was a sacred duty throughout the ancient Near East, so a city’s treatment of guests revealed its moral condition. Lot had moved step by step from pitching his tent toward Sodom (13:12) to living inside it (14:12) and now sitting in its gate. For Israel, hearing this account on the edge of Canaan, the story explained the origins of Moab and Ammon, neighbors east of the Jordan, and warned that the land itself would vomit out peoples who practiced Sodom’s ways (Leviticus 18:24–28; Deuteronomy 29:23).
literaryContext: Chapter 19 is the second panel of a diptych begun in chapter 18. Abraham welcomed the visitors at noon by his tent; Lot receives them at evening in a city gate. The LORD’s promise to “go down now, and see” (18:21) is carried out, and Abraham’s question about ten righteous receives its answer at Lot’s door. Time markers—evening, night, dawn, sunrise, early morning—pace the story from exposure to judgment. Key words bind it together: “know,” “press,” “escape” (a sound play on Lot’s name), and “overthrow,” which becomes Scripture’s standing term for Sodom’s fate. Echoes of the flood are strong: God destroys, rains judgment, and remembers His servant, and the closing episode of drunkenness in the cave recalls Noah’s shame (9:20–27). The chapter closes Lot’s story with the origins of two nations, preparing for Abraham’s own lapse and Isaac’s birth in chapters 20–21.
themes: God’s careful and righteous judgment of sin
Mercy that takes hold of the hesitant
The cost of compromise with a corrupt culture
The urgency of leaving without looking back
Grace that reaches beyond shameful origins

outline.title: Evening Welcome at Sodom’s Gate
outline.summary: Lot meets the two angels at the gate and urges them to shelter in his house, echoing Abraham’s hospitality on a smaller scale.

outline.title: The Night Siege of Lot’s House
outline.summary: The whole city surrounds the house to abuse the guests, Lot makes a desperate and wrongful offer, and the angels rescue him and strike the mob with blindness.

outline.title: Warning, Lingering, and Rescue
outline.summary: The angels announce judgment, the sons-in-law mock, and the LORD in mercy drags Lot’s family out and grants his plea for Zoar.

outline.title: Fire from Heaven and Abraham’s Witness
outline.summary: The LORD overthrows the cities with burning sulfur, Lot’s wife perishes looking back, and Abraham sees the smoke as God remembers him and spares Lot.

outline.title: The Cave and the Birth of Moab and Ammon
outline.summary: Isolated in a cave, Lot’s daughters make him drunk and conceive by him, and their sons become the ancestors of Moab and Ammon.

verses.bibleText: And there came two angels to Sodom at even; and Lot sat in the gate of Sodom: and Lot seeing them rose up to meet them; and he bowed himself with his face toward the ground;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And there came two angels to Sodom at even.” The Hebrew has the article, “the two angels,” pointing back to the pair who left Abraham’s tent while the LORD remained to hear his intercession (18:22). In chapter 18 the narrator called them “men”; here the same visitors are named by their office. Their word describes someone sent on another’s business, and their business is grave: to confirm the outcry that has reached heaven (18:20–21). The road from the heights near Hebron down to the plain was long and steep, yet they arrive that same evening, a hint that their errand is no ordinary journey.

The time stamp matters. Abraham welcomed his guests in the full light of midday; Sodom receives them as darkness falls. The chapter will move from evening through night to dawn and sunrise, and the gathering dark of this first scene suits the moral condition about to be exposed.

Lot is found “in the gate of Sodom.” The gate complex of an ancient town was its civic heart, where elders heard disputes, transactions were witnessed, and news passed from mouth to mouth (Ruth 4:1–11; Deuteronomy 21:19). Lot’s story can be traced through his addresses: he pitched his tent toward Sodom (13:12), then dwelt in it (14:12), and now sits among its prominent men. Whatever office he held, the man who once chose the well-watered plain by sight has settled into its public life.

Yet Lot still bears the marks of Abraham’s household. He rises, goes to meet the strangers, and bows with his face to the ground, the same courtesy his uncle showed hours earlier (18:2). In a city that will soon prove hostile to outsiders, this welcome is the first sign that Lot is not wholly one with his neighbors. Peter would later call him “just Lot,” vexed by what he saw and heard (2 Peter 2:7–8). His faith had been compromised, but it had not been extinguished.

wordNotes.term: מַלְאָכִים (mal’akhim) — angels
wordNotes.explanation: The noun means a messenger, one sent with a commission, and can describe human envoys (Genesis 32:3) as well as heavenly ones. The context shows these are heavenly beings who appeared as men (18:2) and act with divine power (19:11). The Septuagint renders the word ἄγγελοι (angeloi), which likewise means “messengers” and gives English its word “angel.”

wordNotes.term: בְּשַׁעַר־סְדֹם (besha‘ar-sedom) — in the gate of Sodom
wordNotes.explanation: The gate was the place of judgment, commerce, and public counsel. To sit there implied standing in the community, perhaps a place among the elders. The phrase measures how far Lot has traveled from the tent life of his uncle.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Behold now, my lords, turn in, I pray you, into your servant's house, and tarry all night, and wash your feet, and ye shall rise up early, and go on your ways. And they said, Nay; but we will abide in the street all night.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Lot’s invitation reproduces the pattern of Abraham’s welcome in miniature: a respectful address, an offer of rest, water for dusty feet, and freedom to leave early (compare 18:3–5). “Behold now, my lords” treats the visitors as honored travelers. Lot does not yet know who they are; he sees strangers at nightfall in a city where strangers are not safe.

The detail “ye shall rise up early, and go on your ways” may carry more than courtesy. Lot seems eager for his guests to slip in and out of Sodom before its citizens notice them. An old man in Gibeah would later urge a traveling Levite not to spend the night in the open square (Judges 19:20), and that later story shows exactly what Lot feared.

The angels’ refusal is unexpected: “Nay; but we will abide in the street all night.” They had accepted Abraham’s hospitality at once. Here their reluctance tests the sincerity of the host and also positions them to see the city as it truly is. The open square, ordinarily a tolerable place for travelers in a mild climate (compare 28:11), is precisely where the inquiry promised in 18:21 could be carried out.

Hospitality in Scripture is a form of righteousness, not a social nicety. Job counted it among the marks of an upright life that no stranger lodged in the street while his door stood open to the traveler (Job 31:32). The contrast between Lot’s door and Sodom’s street is the hinge on which the night will turn.

wordNotes.term: הִנֶּה־נָּא אֲדֹנַי (hinneh-na adonai) — behold now, my lords
wordNotes.explanation: The vowel pointing here marks an ordinary plural of courtesy addressed to men. In verse 18 Lot uses the form pointed as the divine title, the name reserved for God. The shift traces Lot’s growing recognition of whom he is addressing.

wordNotes.term: בָרְחוֹב (vareḥov) — in the street
wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes the broad open plaza, usually near the gate, where travelers without a host might pass the night. It recurs in the Gibeah account, where a stranger sits in the square until an old man warns him to come indoors.

verses.bibleText: And he pressed upon them greatly; and they turned in unto him, and entered into his house; and he made them a feast, and did bake unleavened bread, and they did eat.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“He pressed upon them greatly.” Lot’s insistence overcomes the angels’ reluctance, and they turn in to his house. The Hebrew verb for pressing reappears in verse 9, where the mob “pressed sore upon” Lot himself. The narrator lets one word frame two kinds of urgency: a host determined to shelter his guests and a city determined to seize them.

Lot “made them a feast, and did bake unleavened bread.” The word for feast usually means a banquet with drink, but the only food named is bread made without leaven, the kind that could be baked quickly for unexpected company. Abraham’s table was described in loving detail—fine meal, a tender calf, butter and milk (18:6–8). Lot’s is sketched in a single line. The comparison is gentle but real: Lot shares his uncle’s instinct for welcome without his uncle’s lavish attentiveness.

Bread without leaven, eaten on a night of deliverance before a hurried departure at dawn, will later become part of Israel’s Passover memory (Exodus 12:39). The narrator draws no explicit line between the two, and it should not be pressed, yet the pattern of a household sheltered indoors while judgment gathers outside does recur in Israel’s story. Centuries later, on the road to Emmaus, the risen Christ, unrecognized at first, yielded to the urging of two disciples and broke bread at their table (Luke 24:29–30). God often meets those who open their doors.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּפְצַר (wayyiftsar) — and he pressed
wordNotes.explanation: The verb describes urging that will not accept a refusal. It describes Jacob urging Esau to accept his gift and Naaman urging Elisha to take a present. In 19:9 the same root describes the mob’s violent pressure, so context decides whether the pressing is generous or hostile.

wordNotes.term: מִשְׁתֶּה (mishteh) — a feast
wordNotes.explanation: Formed from the verb “to drink,” the noun ordinarily denotes a banquet (21:8; 29:22). Here it is paired with מַצּוֹת (matsot), unleavened cakes, suggesting a sincere but hurried meal rather than the elaborate preparation Abraham made.

verses.bibleText: But before they lay down, the men of the city, even the men of Sodom, compassed the house round, both old and young, all the people from every quarter:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But before they lay down”—the evening calm of the household is broken. The narrator piles up phrases to show who surrounds the house. They are the city’s men, Sodom’s own citizens; they come “both old and young”; they are “all the people,” gathered “from every quarter.” Naming the old and the young is a Hebrew way of saying everyone, and the closing phrase can mean “to the last man.” The repetition is deliberate. Abraham’s intercession had descended from fifty righteous to ten (18:32). The scene at Lot’s door supplies the answer: no group of ten stands apart from the crowd. Apart from Lot’s household, the city is united in evil.

This is not the sin of a few dissolute individuals tolerated by a decent majority. Elders who should have restrained the young stand beside them; the young who should have been taught have learned the city’s ways. The narrator had already said that “the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly” (13:13). Now that verdict is displayed in public action, at night, in the open, with no voice among them raised in protest. Wickedness has become the city’s shared culture rather than its shame. The judgment that follows will be total because the corruption is total, a pattern seen before the flood, when “all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth” (6:12).

The image of a whole community encircling a house where guests have taken refuge has a sobering afterlife in Scripture. In Judges 19:22 men of Gibeah, an Israelite town, beset a house in almost identical words. Israel itself could become Sodom. The prophets later used the name for Jerusalem when its leaders abandoned justice (Isaiah 1:10; Jeremiah 23:14). Sodom therefore stands less as a remote foreign city than as a warning of what any society becomes when God is forgotten and appetite rules.

wordNotes.term: מִנַּעַר וְעַד־זָקֵן (minna‘ar we‘ad-zaqen) — both old and young
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “from youth even to old man.” Hebrew often expresses totality by naming two extremes, as with “small and great” in 19:11. The phrase leaves no part of the male population outside the mob.

wordNotes.term: מִקָּצֶה (miqqatseh) — from every quarter
wordNotes.explanation: The word means “from the end” or “from the edge,” picturing men gathered from the farthest corners of the town. Joined with “all the people,” it underscores the city’s unanimous involvement in the assault.

verses.bibleText: And they called unto Lot, and said unto him, Where are the men which came in to thee this night? bring them out unto us, that we may know them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The mob calls for the visitors: “bring them out unto us, that we may know them.” The Hebrew verb “know” can describe ordinary acquaintance, but it is also the Bible’s modest term for sexual union (4:1). Lot’s reply in verse 8, offering daughters “which have not known man,” removes any doubt about the meaning here. The men of Sodom intend to violate the strangers by force.

Several evils converge in this demand. It is an assault on guests, a deliberate trampling of the duty to protect those who come under one’s roof. It is violent coercion—gang rape, meant to dominate and humiliate. And it is homosexual in its aim, contrary to the order God established when He made humanity male and female and joined them in marriage (1:27; 2:24). Moses’ law would later call such relations an abomination (Leviticus 18:22), and Jude recalls that Sodom and the cities around it gave themselves to fornication and went after “strange flesh” (Jude 1:7). Ezekiel names the roots from which these fruits grew: pride, fullness of bread, idle ease, and a refusal to strengthen the poor and needy (Ezekiel 16:49–50). Sodom’s sin was not one thing. Arrogance, prosperity without compassion, contempt for the stranger, and sexual violence form one tangled whole.

Holding these together guards against two errors. One reduces Sodom to a lesson in bad manners and ignores what the text says about sexual violation and God’s design. The other isolates a single sin and forgets that the same prophets who condemned Sodom’s lust also condemned its greed and indifference. Scripture refuses to let any reader feel safely distant from Sodom.

The gospel speaks into this darkness with both truth and hope. Paul lists sexual sins, homosexual practice among them, alongside theft, greed, drunkenness, and slander, and then tells the Corinthians, “such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus” (1 Corinthians 6:11). The cry of Sodom was heard in heaven because God takes the abuse of the vulnerable seriously. The same God sent His Son so that no sinner who turns to Him need share Sodom’s end.

wordNotes.term: וְנֵדְעָה אֹתָם (wened‘ah otam) — that we may know them
wordNotes.explanation: The verb יָדַע (yada‘) ranges from perceiving a fact to intimate personal knowledge. In settings like 4:1 and 19:8 it refers to sexual relations. The cohortative form expresses the mob’s resolve. The same verb returns in 19:33 and 35, where Lot “perceived not,” a painful echo in the chapter’s final scene.

verses.bibleText: And Lot went out at the door unto them, and shut the door after him,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Lot “went out at the door unto them, and shut the door after him.” Hebrew uses two different words here. The first is the doorway, the opening of the house; the second is the door itself, the hinged panel that can be closed and barred. Lot steps through the opening and closes the panel behind him, placing his own body between the crowd and his guests.

The act takes courage. Lot is outnumbered by a mob that has thrown off every restraint, and he chooses to face it alone rather than let it reach those in his care. The door becomes the dividing line of the whole scene. The crowd will press against it (v. 9); the angels will pull Lot back through it and shut it (v. 10); the blinded men will grope for it in vain (v. 11). What Lot cannot accomplish by standing in the doorway, God will accomplish through it. Jesus would later call Himself the door through which the sheep find safety (John 10:9), and the true shelter of this night lies in the presence of God’s messengers within.

wordNotes.term: הַפֶּתְחָה … וְהַדֶּלֶת (happetḥah … wehaddelet) — at the door … the door
wordNotes.explanation: פֶּתַח (petaḥ) is the entrance or opening, as in “the tent door” of 18:1; דֶּלֶת (delet) is the hinged leaf that closes it. The distinction shows Lot standing in the opening and shutting the panel behind him to keep the mob from his guests.

verses.bibleText: And said, I pray you, brethren, do not so wickedly.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Lot pleads, “I pray you, brethren, do not so wickedly.” The address “brethren” is striking. Lot speaks to the mob as kinsmen and fellow citizens, hoping that a sense of belonging will soften them. His years in Sodom show in that word; he has come to think of these men as his own. Yet his plea also names their intention for what it is. He calls it wicked, and in doing so he judges by a standard higher than the city’s customs. Whatever Sodom approved, Lot knew that God did not.

The appeal is brief and courteous, built around the Hebrew particle of entreaty. There is no threat in it and no mention of the LORD. Lot argues as a neighbor, not as a prophet. Abraham had reasoned with God from His justice (18:25); Lot reasons with sinners from their goodwill and discovers that it does not exist. His failure is instructive. A believer who has blended into a culture may still see evil clearly, yet carry little moral weight with those he has tried to resemble (compare Proverbs 25:26). Peter’s portrait of Lot fits this moment: a righteous man whose soul was vexed from day to day by the lawless deeds around him (2 Peter 2:8).

wordNotes.term: אַל־נָא אַחַי תָּרֵעוּ (al-na aḥai tare‘u) — I pray you, brethren, do not so wickedly
wordNotes.explanation: The verb רָעַע (ra‘a‘) means to do evil or inflict harm; the same form appears in the command “do my prophets no harm.” In verse 9 the crowd answers with the same root, “now will we deal worse with thee.” Lot names their act as evil, and they turn the word back on him as a threat.

verses.bibleText: Behold now, I have two daughters which have not known man; let me, I pray you, bring them out unto you, and do ye to them as is good in your eyes: only unto these men do nothing; for therefore came they under the shadow of my roof.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Lot’s next words are among the most troubling in Genesis. “I have two daughters which have not known man; let me, I pray you, bring them out unto you, and do ye to them as is good in your eyes.” To protect his guests, Lot offers his own unmarried daughters to the mob.

The narrator records the offer without approving it, and nothing in Scripture gives it warrant. Lot’s reason is stated: “for therefore came they under the shadow of my roof.” In the ancient world a host was bound to protect those who entered his house, even at the cost of his own life. That sense of obligation explains why Lot is desperate; it does not excuse what he proposes. His daughters are not property to be traded for the safety of others. They bear God’s image as surely as his guests do (1:27), and a father’s first duty was to shield them (compare Deuteronomy 22:25–27). The obligation to his guests could have been met by offering himself; instead he offers those who most depended on him. The angels will intervene before the offer can be carried out, but the willingness itself exposes how far Sodom had bent Lot’s moral judgment.

There is irony in the phrase “as is good in your eyes.” Lot hands the definition of good to a crowd that has already shown it calls evil good. The same expression marks the lawless days of the judges, when “every man did that which was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25), and the parallel story at Gibeah ends in horror when a concubine is actually thrust outside (Judges 19:24–28). Genesis shows how close Lot came to that horror.

Readers should feel the weight of this verse rather than explain it away. Scripture tells the truth about its saints, and here it shows a man whom God still calls righteous (2 Peter 2:7) making a choice that wrongs the vulnerable. His deliverance in the following verses is pure mercy. For anyone who has been harmed by someone who should have protected them, the text does not hide the wrong. God sees the daughters behind that door, and His messengers act before the mob can touch them. The Lord who later called fathers not to provoke their children and husbands to love as Christ loved the church (Ephesians 5:25; 6:4) never sanctioned what Lot offered.

wordNotes.term: בְּצֵל קֹרָתִי (betsel qorati) — under the shadow of my roof
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “in the shade of my beam.” Shade is a common biblical picture of protection, as in the shadow of the Almighty or the bramble’s offer of shelter in Jotham’s fable. Lot appeals to the protection his house owes its guests, yet the same image condemns his willingness to send his daughters out from under it.

wordNotes.term: כַּטּוֹב בְּעֵינֵיכֶם (kattov be‘eineikhem) — as is good in your eyes
wordNotes.explanation: The idiom hands another person the right to decide what to do, as Abram did with Sarai concerning Hagar. Spoken to a violent mob, it surrenders moral judgment to men who have rejected God’s standard and anticipates the refrain of the book of Judges.

verses.bibleText: And they said, Stand back. And they said again, This one fellow came in to sojourn, and he will needs be a judge: now will we deal worse with thee, than with them. And they pressed sore upon the man, even Lot, and came near to break the door.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The crowd’s answer is contempt: “Stand back.” Then they turn on Lot himself: “This one fellow came in to sojourn, and he will needs be a judge.” In their eyes Lot is still an immigrant, a resident alien who has been permitted to live among them and now presumes to correct them. Whatever standing he had gained at the gate counts for nothing once he opposes their will. The man who called them “brethren” is reminded that he was never truly one of them.

The complaint that he “will needs be a judge” is literally “he keeps on judging,” suggesting this was not the first time Lot had spoken against their ways. His vexation of soul (2 Peter 2:8) had apparently found its way into words, and the city resented it. A similar taunt would one day be flung at Moses: “Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?” (Exodus 2:14). Those who set themselves against God’s order often treat any moral word as an intrusion.

“Now will we deal worse with thee, than with them.” The crowd’s fury turns from the strangers to their protector. They press hard against Lot and come near to breaking the door. The verb of pressing is the one used when Lot urged his guests to stay (v. 3). The scene has become a siege.

Humanly speaking, Lot has reached the end: his appeal has failed, his compromise has been scorned, and his own life is in danger. Only now does heaven act. God often allows human resources to run out so that His deliverance cannot be mistaken for anything else (2 Corinthians 1:9–10). Sodom imagined that the stranger in its midst was playing the judge; the true Judge of all the earth (18:25) is already behind the door.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׁפֹּט שָׁפוֹט (wayyishpot shafot) — and he will needs be a judge
wordNotes.explanation: The finite verb is intensified by an infinitive of the same root, a Hebrew way of stressing an action: “he keeps judging” or “he insists on judging.” The mob mocks Lot’s moral protest as the meddling of an outsider, much as the Hebrew in Egypt resented Moses’ intervention.

wordNotes.term: לָגוּר (lagur) — to sojourn
wordNotes.explanation: The verb גּוּר (gur) describes living as a resident foreigner without the rights of a native. Abraham accepted that status as a pilgrim in the land; Lot had tried to leave it behind, yet the city still regarded him as an outsider.

verses.bibleText: But the men put forth their hand, and pulled Lot into the house to them, and shut to the door.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But the men put forth their hand, and pulled Lot into the house to them, and shut to the door.” The roles reverse in a single sentence. Lot went out to protect his guests; now his guests protect him. The visitors he thought he was sheltering are the ones who shelter him. The narrator still calls them “the men,” keeping their outward appearance in view, but their action reveals their authority.

The same hands will reach out again at dawn to take hold of Lot, his wife, and his daughters and bring them out of the city (v. 16). Rescue in this chapter is repeatedly physical and decisive: Lot is drawn in, then drawn out. He contributes little but his need. The picture fits the psalmist’s testimony, “He sent from above, he took me, he drew me out of many waters” (Psalm 18:16). The door the mob nearly broke is now shut by heavenly hands, much as the door of the ark was shut by the LORD Himself when judgment was about to fall (7:16).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׁלְחוּ … אֶת־יָדָם (wayyishleḥu … et-yadam) — put forth their hand
wordNotes.explanation: “To send out the hand” is a common Hebrew idiom for decisive action, whether to take hold, to harm, or to rescue. Noah put forth his hand to bring the dove into the ark; here the angels do the same for Lot, a gesture of protective intervention.

verses.bibleText: And they smote the men that were at the door of the house with blindness, both small and great: so that they wearied themselves to find the door.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The angels “smote the men that were at the door of the house with blindness, both small and great.” The word for blindness here is rare. It appears elsewhere only when the LORD strikes the Syrian army at Elisha’s request (2 Kings 6:18), and in both places it describes a sudden, supernatural confusion more than ordinary loss of sight. The men “wearied themselves to find the door”: they groped and stumbled, unable to locate the very entrance they had been about to smash.

The phrase “small and great” matches “old and young” in verse 4. The whole crowd that gathered in unity of purpose is now united in helplessness. The judgment is still restrained—no one dies at the door—but it is a sign of what is coming. Those who would not see the evil of their deeds are given over to a blindness that mirrors their condition. Elsewhere in Scripture spiritual blindness is both a sin and a judgment (Isaiah 6:9–10; Romans 1:21).

The startling detail is that the blinded men keep trying. Even under a miraculous stroke they neither repent nor flee; they exhaust themselves still seeking the door. Sin that has hardened into habit does not easily let go. For Lot, the miracle confirms who his guests are: the visitors in his house have power to close eyes as well as open them. In a later day the Lord Jesus would give sight to the blind and warn that those who claim to see may be the blindest of all (John 9:39–41).

wordNotes.term: בַּסַּנְוֵרִים (bassanwerim) — with blindness
wordNotes.explanation: This uncommon term differs from the ordinary Hebrew word for blindness. Its only other use involves God confusing an army’s perception, so the sense appears to be a dazzling, bewildering stroke that left the men disoriented rather than simply sightless.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּלְאוּ (wayyil’u) — wearied themselves
wordNotes.explanation: The verb describes exhaustion that comes from futile effort. The prophets use it of people who tire themselves in pursuits that cannot succeed, including those who weary themselves to commit iniquity.

verses.bibleText: And the men said unto Lot, Hast thou here any besides? son in law, and thy sons, and thy daughters, and whatsoever thou hast in the city, bring them out of this place:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Now the visitors disclose their errand. “Hast thou here any besides? son in law, and thy sons, and thy daughters, and whatsoever thou hast in the city, bring them out of this place.” Before announcing destruction, they offer rescue. Mercy speaks first. The question opens the circle of deliverance as wide as Lot’s household reaches, naming even sons-in-law before sons.

This follows the pattern of the flood, when Noah’s sons and their wives entered the ark with him (7:1, 7), and it anticipates the scarlet cord in Rahab’s window, by which her whole household was spared when Jericho fell (Joshua 2:18–19). God’s judgments in Scripture are never indiscriminate. He distinguishes between those who will leave the doomed place and those who will not, and He gives each a real opportunity. Abraham had asked, “Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked?” (18:23). The angels’ question is part of the answer.

“Bring them out of this place” sounds a call that echoes across the Bible: come away from a world under judgment. Revelation issues the same summons for the last days: “Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues” (Revelation 18:4). The invitation is urgent precisely because it is gracious. God is not willing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9), but He will not force anyone out of the city they love.

wordNotes.term: חָתָן (ḥatan) — son in law
wordNotes.explanation: The term covers a man related by marriage, including a bridegroom or one formally pledged to a daughter. Its inclusion shows the angels extending the offer of rescue even to prospective in-laws, treating them as part of Lot’s family.

verses.bibleText: For we will destroy this place, because the cry of them is waxen great before the face of the LORD; and the LORD hath sent us to destroy it.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For we will destroy this place, because the cry of them is waxen great before the face of the LORD.” The angels speak as agents. The participle “we will destroy” suggests something already in motion and about to happen. The verb for destroying is the one used of the flood, when God saw that the earth was corrupt and declared that He would destroy it (6:13, 17). Sodom is a smaller, localized repetition of that earlier judgment.

The reason given is “the cry of them.” In 18:20–21 the LORD spoke of the outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah and said, “I will go down now, and see.” The word describes the cry of the oppressed and wronged, like Abel’s blood crying from the ground (4:10) or Israel groaning under Egyptian bondage (Exodus 3:7). God’s judgment answers suffering. The victims of Sodom, unnamed in Genesis, had called out, and heaven heard.

The night’s events have served as the inquiry. God does not condemn on rumor; He came down to see, and two witnesses have watched the whole city gather at the door (compare Deuteronomy 19:15). This is a careful picture of divine justice: patient, informed, and righteous when it acts. The final judgment shares that character. The heavenly court sits and the books are opened before sentence is carried out (Daniel 7:9–10), so that the redeemed can confess, “true and righteous are thy judgments” (Revelation 16:7).

“The LORD hath sent us to destroy it.” The angels claim no authority of their own. The destruction is the LORD’s work, carried out by servants who do His commandments and hearken to the voice of His word (Psalm 103:20).

wordNotes.term: צַעֲקָתָם (tsa‘aqatam) — the cry of them
wordNotes.explanation: The noun describes a loud cry of distress or a plea for help, especially from those who have been wronged. Here it most likely means the cry raised against Sodom by its victims, the same outcry the LORD said He would investigate.

wordNotes.term: מַשְׁחִתִים (mashḥitim) — we will destroy
wordNotes.explanation: From שָׁחַת (shaḥat), to ruin or corrupt. The same root describes both the earth’s corruption and God’s destroying it in the flood narrative, so what has become corrupt is finally brought to ruin. Revelation speaks of God destroying those who destroy the earth.

verses.bibleText: And Lot went out, and spake unto his sons in law, which married his daughters, and said, Up, get you out of this place; for the LORD will destroy this city. But he seemed as one that mocked unto his sons in law.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Lot obeys at once. He goes out into the dark streets to his sons-in-law and warns them: “Up, get you out of this place; for the LORD will destroy this city.” He believes the message and acts on it, though it means walking through a city that had just tried to break down his door. Here Lot shows a faith worth noting.

The response is crushing: “he seemed as one that mocked unto his sons in law.” They thought he was joking. The Hebrew word for mocking belongs to the family of words around Isaac’s name, “laughter” (17:17; 18:12; 21:6). Sarah laughed at a promise of life and was gently rebuked; these young men laughed at a warning of death and perished. Their unbelief did not arise because the message was unclear. It arose because the messenger had little credibility. Lot had lived so comfortably within Sodom that a sudden warning of judgment from his lips sounded absurd.

The phrase “which married his daughters” may refer to men who had already married daughters of Lot, or, more likely in view of verse 8, men who were pledged to marry the two daughters still at home. Either way, Lot could not persuade his own family. His influence had been spent long before the crisis came.

Jesus used the days of Lot as a picture of the world before His return: people eating, drinking, buying, selling, planting, and building, untroubled until fire fell (Luke 17:28–29). Peter warned of scoffers who would ask, “Where is the promise of his coming?” (2 Peter 3:3–4). Mockery of coming judgment is nothing new. The faithful witness is the one whose life makes the warning believable before the hour arrives.

wordNotes.term: כִמְצַחֵק (khimtsaḥeq) — as one that mocked
wordNotes.explanation: A participle of צָחַק (tsaḥaq), “to laugh” or “to jest.” The root is used for Sarah’s laughter and Ishmael’s mocking. Here it means the sons-in-law took Lot’s urgent warning as a joke.

wordNotes.term: לֹקְחֵי בְנֹתָיו (loqḥei venotav) — which married his daughters
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “takers of his daughters.” The participle can describe a completed marriage or one already arranged but not yet carried out. Verse 8, which speaks of daughters who have not known a man, suggests the men were betrothed to them, like the man in Deuteronomy who has pledged a wife but not yet taken her.

verses.bibleText: And when the morning arose, then the angels hastened Lot, saying, Arise, take thy wife, and thy two daughters, which are here; lest thou be consumed in the iniquity of the city.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And when the morning arose, then the angels hastened Lot.” Dawn is breaking, and the night of warning has ended. The verb “hastened” implies pressing urgency, the kind that pushes someone who is not moving fast enough. The commands come in quick succession: “Arise, take thy wife, and thy two daughters, which are here.” The words “which are here” confirm that the others—the sons-in-law who mocked—will not come. The rescue party has already shrunk.

“Lest thou be consumed in the iniquity of the city.” The Hebrew word for iniquity can mean both the sin and its penalty, because in Scripture the two belong together (4:13). To remain in Sodom is to share its guilt and its fate. The verb “consumed” is the one Abraham used when he asked whether the LORD would sweep away the righteous with the wicked (18:23–24). The angels’ urgency is God’s answer to that prayer: the righteous will not be swept away, but they must leave.

Divine patience has limits set by divine wisdom. The night of warning was mercy; the dawn brings the deadline. Moses would later urge Israel to depart from the tents of rebels “lest ye be consumed in all their sins” (Numbers 16:26), and Paul presses the same urgency on every hearer of the gospel: “now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).

wordNotes.term: תִּסָּפֶה (tissafeh) — be consumed
wordNotes.explanation: From סָפָה (safah), to sweep away or snatch off. Abraham used it when pleading for the righteous, and Moses uses it when warning Israel away from Korah’s company. Its return here signals that God is honoring Abraham’s concern by removing the righteous before the city is swept away.

wordNotes.term: בַּעֲוֹן הָעִיר (ba‘awon ha‘ir) — in the iniquity of the city
wordNotes.explanation: עָוֹן (‘awon) covers guilt and the punishment that guilt brings. Cain’s cry that his punishment was greater than he could bear uses the same word. To stay is to be caught up in the city’s sin and its consequences.

verses.bibleText: And while he lingered, the men laid hold upon his hand, and upon the hand of his wife, and upon the hand of his two daughters; the LORD being merciful unto him: and they brought him forth, and set him without the city.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And while he lingered.” Few phrases in Genesis are more searching. Lot has been warned by angels, has seen a miracle at his own door, and has himself announced the coming destruction to his sons-in-law. Yet when the moment comes to leave, he hesitates. The Hebrew verb carries the sense of delaying, tarrying, holding back. Perhaps he thought of his house, his flocks, the wealth gathered since the day he chose the well-watered plain (13:10–11). Perhaps he hoped for a little more time. Whatever held him, his heart had roots in Sodom that one night could not tear up.

The angels do not wait for Lot to decide. They seize Lot by the hand, then his wife, then both daughters, and they bring him out and set him outside the city. The rescue is almost forcible. Lot is not dragged against his will, but he is carried past his own indecision. The narrator explains why: “the LORD being merciful unto him.” The word describes compassion that spares, a pity that moves to rescue from danger. Lot’s deliverance does not rest on the strength of his faith or the quality of his choices. It rests on God’s mercy.

This is the gospel in narrative form. Salvation in Scripture is never the reward of the hesitant who finally make themselves worthy. “Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus 3:5). The hands that drew Lot from Sodom picture the grace that takes hold of sinners who cannot free themselves. Zechariah describes God’s people as “a brand plucked out of the fire” (Zechariah 3:2), and Jude urges believers to rescue others in the same way, “pulling them out of the fire” (Jude 1:23).

Yet mercy that takes the hand does not cancel the need for response. The angels set Lot outside the city, but from there he must keep moving. Grace begins the rescue and then calls for continued trust and obedience (Philippians 2:12–13). Lot’s lingering stands as a warning to every believer whose affections remain tied to a world that is passing away (1 John 2:15–17).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּתְמַהְמָהּ (wayyitmahmah) — and while he lingered
wordNotes.explanation: A reflexive form of מָהַהּ (mahah), to delay or hesitate; the doubled syllables suggest dragging delay. Israel, by contrast, left Egypt so urgently that they could not tarry, and the psalmist rejoices that he made haste and delayed not to keep God’s commandments.

wordNotes.term: בְּחֶמְלַת יְהוָה (beḥemlat YHWH) — the LORD being merciful
wordNotes.explanation: חֶמְלָה (ḥemlah) is compassion that spares from harm. The related verb describes Pharaoh’s daughter pitying the infant Moses, and Isaiah uses the word when he says the LORD redeemed His people in His love and in His pity.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when they had brought them forth abroad, that he said, Escape for thy life; look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain; escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Once outside the walls, the instructions come in four short commands: “Escape for thy life; look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain; escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed.” The verb shifts to the singular—“he said”—as one speaker takes the lead. Because Lot answers Him in the next verse with the divine title, the speaker is best understood as the LORD Himself, the same One who had talked with Abraham, whom later revelation shows to be the Son before His incarnation, now joining His messengers to press the urgent call.

“Escape” sounds like Lot’s own name in Hebrew. His very identity is bound up with his need to be delivered. “For thy life” means simply to save his life; the stakes are survival itself. The same verb is used for a fugitive slipping away from an enemy in war, and it suits the moment. There is no time to gather goods or say farewell. The only question is whether Lot will run while the door of mercy stands open.

“Look not behind thee.” The command forbids more than a passing glance. It means not to turn the heart back toward what is being left. To stop, to linger, or to gaze back would be to begin returning. Jesus applied the principle to discipleship: “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62).

“Neither stay thou in all the plain.” The plain that Lot once saw as “the garden of the LORD” (13:10) has become the most dangerous ground on earth. The beauty that first drew him is now the zone of destruction. Safety lies in the mountain, the rugged high country Lot had once turned away from. What looks attractive can prove deadly, and what looks hard can be the place of preservation (Psalm 121:1–2). Paul’s counsel to Timothy carries the same urgency: “Flee also youthful lusts” (2 Timothy 2:22).

wordNotes.term: הִמָּלֵט עַל־נַפְשֶׁךָ (himmalet ‘al-nafshekha) — escape for thy life
wordNotes.explanation: מָלַט (malat) means to slip away or escape, and its sound echoes the name Lot (lot). נֶפֶשׁ (nephesh) here means life itself, the living person who is in danger of dying, not a separate inner entity. The same command is used when David flees from Saul and when Moab’s refugees are told to run.

wordNotes.term: אַל־תַּבִּיט אַחֲרֶיךָ (al-tabbit aḥareikha) — look not behind thee
wordNotes.explanation: נָבַט (nabat) means to look intently or gaze, not merely to glimpse. The same verb describes Abraham looking toward heaven to count the stars, and it returns in verse 26 when Lot’s wife looks back.

verses.bibleText: And Lot said unto them, Oh, not so, my Lord:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Lot said unto them, Oh, not so, my Lord.” At the very moment when obedience requires speed, Lot argues. His first word is a refusal—“not so”—softened by the particle of entreaty. Strikingly, it is the same phrase with which he pleaded with the mob in verse 7. The man who said “please, no” to Sodom’s wickedness now says “please, no” to God’s way of escape.

The address “my Lord” is pointed in the Hebrew text as the divine title, not the ordinary courtesy “my lords” of verse 2. Though the narrator says Lot spoke “unto them,” he directs his words to the LORD, the One who has just commanded him. He knows to whom he speaks, and still he hesitates.

Such resistance often wears a respectful face. Lot does not defy God openly; he negotiates. Like Peter, who answered a heavenly command with “Not so, Lord” (Acts 10:14), Lot shows how a believer can resist a plain word while addressing God reverently. Grace, as the following verses reveal, bears patiently with that weakness.

wordNotes.term: אַל־נָא אֲדֹנָי (al-na adonai) — Oh, not so, my Lord
wordNotes.explanation: Here אֲדֹנָי is pointed with the long vowel that Scripture reserves for God, unlike the courteous plural of verse 2. Abraham used the same divine title when he spoke humbly as dust and ashes. The particle of refusal repeats Lot’s plea to the mob in verse 7.

verses.bibleText: Behold now, thy servant hath found grace in thy sight, and thou hast magnified thy mercy, which thou hast shewed unto me in saving my life; and I cannot escape to the mountain, lest some evil take me, and I die:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Lot’s speech begins with gratitude. “Thy servant hath found grace in thy sight, and thou hast magnified thy mercy, which thou hast shewed unto me in saving my life.” Every phrase is true. He has found grace; the LORD’s steadfast love has been made great toward him; his life has been preserved. These are words Abraham himself might have used (18:3), the vocabulary of covenant faithfulness, the loyal love God shows to those He binds to Himself.

But gratitude turns quickly to fear. “I cannot escape to the mountain, lest some evil take me, and I die.” The God who has just pulled him from a doomed city is now suspected of leading him to his death in the hills. Lot’s fear is not rational. If God can bring him out of Sodom, He can keep him in the mountains. Unbelief often looks prudent while doubting the One who has already proved faithful. Lot even uses the word “evil,” the word he spoke to the mob (v. 7). He fears disaster in the place God appoints more than he ever feared the evil of the place he chose.

The verse captures a pattern every believer recognizes. Thankfulness for past deliverance is easy to express; trust for the next step is harder. Israel on the edge of Canaan feared the land God was giving more than the wilderness behind them (Numbers 14:3). Jesus asked His frightened disciples, “Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?” (Mark 4:40). God’s past mercies are given to steady the soul for future obedience (Psalm 56:3–4).

wordNotes.term: וַתַּגְדֵּל חַסְדְּךָ (wattagdel ḥasdekha) — thou hast magnified thy mercy
wordNotes.explanation: חֶסֶד (ḥesed) is God’s steadfast covenant love, loyal and active. The pairing with “great” belongs to the language of worship, as when the psalmist praises the greatness of God’s mercy toward him or Solomon recalls the great kindness shown to David. Lot speaks the vocabulary of praise, yet his next words show fear outrunning faith.

wordNotes.term: לְהַחֲיוֹת אֶת־נַפְשִׁי (lehaḥayot et-nafshi) — in saving my life
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “to keep my soul alive.” נֶפֶשׁ (nephesh) here is the living person; to save it is to preserve Lot from death. Joseph uses the same causative verb when he says God sent him ahead to save lives, showing that the phrase concerns bodily survival, not an immortal component separate from the body.

verses.bibleText: Behold now, this city is near to flee unto, and it is a little one: Oh, let me escape thither, (is it not a little one?) and my soul shall live.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Behold now, this city is near to flee unto, and it is a little one: Oh, let me escape thither, (is it not a little one?) and my soul shall live.” Lot proposes an alternative of his own. Instead of the mountain, he asks for a small town nearby, one of the cities of the plain, earlier called Bela (14:2). His argument is that it is close and that it is small. The repeated “is it not a little one?” sounds almost like bargaining: surely a small exception will not matter.

The contrast with Abraham is plain. Abraham pleaded for an entire city on the basis of God’s justice and the righteous within it (18:23–32). Lot pleads for a small city on the basis of his own convenience. Abraham’s prayer looked outward; Lot’s looks inward. Even now Lot cannot imagine life apart from city walls. He has been taken out of Sodom, but the habits of Sodom have not yet been taken out of him. His request is not rebellion so much as a refusal to let God decide the shape of his safety.

“My soul shall live” means “I shall stay alive.” Abram had used the very same words when he asked Sarai to say she was his sister, “and my soul shall live because of thee” (12:13). Scripture’s language of the soul is whole-person language: a living soul is a living being (2:7), and the soul that lives is the person who does not die.

What follows carries a lesson. God grants the request, but the town Lot chose will not hold him for long (v. 30). The places we pick for comfort can fail us, while the places God appoints are safe even when they look hard. “Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding” (Proverbs 3:5).

wordNotes.term: מִצְעָר (mits‘ar) — a little one
wordNotes.explanation: The word means small or insignificant, as when Bildad tells Job his beginning was small. It sounds like the name Zoar given in verse 22, so the town’s very name preserves the memory of Lot’s plea.

wordNotes.term: וּתְחִי נַפְשִׁי (uteḥi nafshi) — and my soul shall live
wordNotes.explanation: The idiom means “so that I may live.” Abram used it when he feared for his life in Egypt. The soul in such phrases is the person’s life, which can be preserved or lost, as Ezekiel affirms when he says the soul that sins shall die.

verses.bibleText: And he said unto him, See, I have accepted thee concerning this thing also, that I will not overthrow this city, for the which thou hast spoken.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The answer is astonishing: “See, I have accepted thee concerning this thing also, that I will not overthrow this city, for the which thou hast spoken.” God does not rebuke Lot’s weak faith. He grants the request. The word “also” is pointed: in addition to every mercy already shown—the warning, the protection, the hands that drew him out—God adds yet another. Zoar, otherwise destined for the same overthrow, is spared for Lot’s sake.

The Hebrew idiom behind “I have accepted thee” is literally “I have lifted up thy face.” It pictures a superior raising the face of someone bowed low in petition and granting his request. A form of the same language appears in the priestly blessing, “The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee” (Numbers 6:24–26), where it describes God’s favor turned toward His people.

The verse reveals how the LORD bears with imperfect people. He accommodates Lot’s fear without approving it. Lot’s prayer was small and self-centered, yet God listened. This is no endorsement of the plea; it is a revelation of the generosity of God, who “knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14). The same patience meets every believer whose faith is weaker than it should be. The God who spared Zoar for a hesitant man sustains those who come to Him in weakness through Christ, the High Priest touched with the feeling of our infirmities (Hebrews 4:15–16). And it reminds us that the prayer of a righteous person, however flawed, can affect an entire town (James 5:16).

wordNotes.term: נָשָׂאתִי פָנֶיךָ (nasa’ti faneikha) — I have accepted thee
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “I have lifted up thy face,” an idiom for showing favor and granting a petition. The same idiom describes the LORD accepting Job’s intercession for his friends, and a related expression appears in the priestly blessing.

wordNotes.term: לְבִלְתִּי הָפְכִּי (levilti hofki) — that I will not overthrow
wordNotes.explanation: הָפַךְ (hafakh) means to overturn or turn upside down. It is the key verb of the chapter’s judgment (vv. 25, 29) and becomes Scripture’s standard expression for Sodom’s fate.

verses.bibleText: Haste thee, escape thither; for I cannot do any thing till thou be come thither. Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Haste thee, escape thither; for I cannot do any thing till thou be come thither.” The command to hurry returns, but now the reason is remarkable. The LORD says He cannot act until Lot is safe. The inability is not a lack of power but the binding force of God’s own purpose and promise. Having committed Himself to deliver the righteous, He will not let judgment fall while His servant is still exposed. Here is the answer to Abraham’s question in its fullest form: the Judge of all the earth will not destroy the righteous with the wicked (18:25).

A parallel appears in John’s vision of four angels holding back the winds of the earth until the servants of God are sealed in their foreheads (Revelation 7:1–3). Judgment waits on the security of God’s people. Even the flood did not begin until Noah was inside the ark and the LORD had shut him in (7:16).

“Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar.” The name sounds like Lot’s word “little” (v. 20). Every later mention of Zoar would recall the frightened man who pleaded for a small place and received it. The town survived for a time and appears at the edge of Moses’ view of the promised land (Deuteronomy 34:3) and in Isaiah’s lament over Moab (Isaiah 15:5).

wordNotes.term: לֹא אוּכַל (lo’ ukhal) — I cannot
wordNotes.explanation: The same words Lot used in verse 19, “I cannot escape.” Lot’s “cannot” springs from fear; the LORD’s springs from faithfulness to His own word. Paul affirms that God cannot deny Himself.

wordNotes.term: צוֹעַר (Tso‘ar) — Zoar
wordNotes.explanation: The name means “little” or “small,” echoing Lot’s plea about “a little one.” The town lay at the southern edge of the plain and is later remembered as a landmark in Moses’ view from Pisgah and in the prophets’ oracles about Moab.

verses.bibleText: The sun was risen upon the earth when Lot entered into Zoar.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“The sun was risen upon the earth when Lot entered into Zoar.” The brief note marks the turning point. The angels arrived at evening (v. 1); the mob came by night (v. 4); the warning was pressed at dawn (v. 15); and now the sun has risen as Lot reaches safety. The movement from darkness to full light frames the night of Sodom’s exposure and the morning of its judgment.

In the ancient world sunrise was linked with justice, the hour when courts sat and wrongs were brought to light. Zephaniah says that every morning the LORD brings His judgment to light (Zephaniah 3:5), and Malachi pictures the Sun of righteousness rising with healing for those who fear God’s name, while the proud are burned as stubble (Malachi 4:1–2). The same sunrise means rescue for Lot and ruin for Sodom. When God’s day dawns, it brings terror or hope depending on where one stands.

wordNotes.term: הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ יָצָא (hashemesh yatsa’) — the sun was risen
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the sun went forth.” The same idiom describes the sun coming out like a bridegroom and the faithful shining like the sun when he goes forth in his might. Here the rising sun marks the hour of judgment.

verses.bibleText: Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven.” The sentence opens emphatically with “the LORD” and closes with “from the LORD,” so that God frames the judgment on both sides. Whatever natural means may have been involved, the narrator leaves no doubt about its source. This is no accident of geology or blind force of nature. It is the deliberate act of the Judge of all the earth.

The verb “rained” is the one used of the flood (7:4). The God who once opened the windows of heaven to send water now sends fire. “Brimstone and fire” most likely describes burning sulfur. The region around the southern Dead Sea is rich in bitumen and sulfurous deposits (compare 14:10), and God may have used such materials in an extraordinary way. Yet the timing—after Lot entered Zoar and not before—shows that the event was governed by God’s word, not by chance.

The doubled name has drawn the attention of Christian readers: “the LORD rained … from the LORD.” In ordinary Hebrew style it underlines the divine source. Yet in the light of fuller revelation, the LORD who stood on earth speaking with Abraham and the LORD in heaven from whom the fire came are distinguished without being divided, a hint of the plurality within the one God that the New Testament makes plain (compare Zechariah 2:8–11; John 5:22).

Sodom’s overthrow became Scripture’s classic picture of judgment by fire. Jesus compared the day of His return to it (Luke 17:29–30). Peter says God turned the cities into ashes, “making them an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly” (2 Peter 2:6). Jude says they are “set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire” (Jude 1:7). The fire is called eternal because its result is permanent; the cities are not still burning. So it will be at the final judgment: the wicked are not kept alive in endless torment but are consumed and become ashes (Malachi 4:1, 3). God’s fire brings sin and sinners to an end so that a cleansed new earth can follow (2 Peter 3:10–13).

wordNotes.term: וַיהוָה הִמְטִיר (wayhwh himtir) — then the LORD rained
wordNotes.explanation: The causative form of מָטַר (matar), “to rain.” God uses the same verb when He announces the flood and when He promises to rain bread from heaven in the wilderness. The LORD who sends rain in blessing can also send it in judgment.

wordNotes.term: גָּפְרִית וָאֵשׁ (gofrit wa’esh) — brimstone and fire
wordNotes.explanation: גָּפְרִית (gofrit) is sulfur; with “fire” the pair likely means burning sulfur. After this event the phrase becomes part of the Bible’s vocabulary for divine judgment on the wicked, in the Psalms and the prophets alike.

verses.bibleText: And he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew upon the ground.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew upon the ground.” The list moves from cities to region, from people to plants. Nothing is left. The word “overthrew” means to turn upside down, to reverse completely. It becomes the Bible’s standard term for Sodom’s fate, and the phrase “as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah” echoes through the prophets (Isaiah 13:19; Jeremiah 49:18; Amos 4:11).

The destruction reaches beyond the two cities named. Deuteronomy adds Admah and Zeboim (Deuteronomy 29:23; compare Hosea 11:8), and Jude speaks of “the cities about them” (Jude 1:7). Only Zoar was spared, and that for Lot’s sake.

There is grim irony in the words “all the plain.” The plain was what Lot had chosen when he lifted up his eyes and saw that it was well watered everywhere, “even as the garden of the LORD” (13:10). The narrator had noted then that this was before the LORD destroyed Sodom. Now the garden-like valley becomes a wasteland, a reversal of Eden. Moses would warn Israel that their own land could become “brimstone, and salt, and burning, that it is not sown, nor beareth” if they forsook the covenant (Deuteronomy 29:23).

The thoroughness of the judgment underscores its finality. Sodom does not return, and its people are given no further probation. Their case awaits the final judgment, where Jesus says it will be more tolerable for Sodom than for the towns that rejected His own ministry (Matthew 11:23–24). God judges according to the light each has received, and that day will display both His justice and His fairness.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּהֲפֹךְ (wayyahafokh) — and he overthrew
wordNotes.explanation: From הָפַךְ (hafakh), to overturn. Lamentations says Sodom was overthrown “as in a moment,” and Jeremiah curses the day of his birth by wishing it were like the cities the LORD overthrew without pity. The word stresses sudden and total reversal.

wordNotes.term: הַכִּכָּר (hakkikkar) — the plain
wordNotes.explanation: The noun means a round area or circuit, here the district of the Jordan around the cities. It is the word used when Lot surveyed the land and chose “all the plain of Jordan,” so its repetition recalls the fateful choice.

verses.bibleText: But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.” The verse is brief and unforgettable. Lot’s wife is never named, yet her end became one of Scripture’s best-known warnings. Walking behind her husband, outside the city, with deliverance nearly complete, she did what the LORD had forbidden (v. 17). She looked back.

The verb is the strong one used in the command: not a passing glance but a deliberate, lingering gaze. Her body had left Sodom; her heart had not. Her home, her possessions, perhaps married children and friends were still there. She looked back with longing toward everything she was losing, and in that moment she was overtaken by the judgment falling on the plain. Becoming “a pillar of salt” likely means she was caught in the rain of salt and sulfur and encrusted where she stood, a lasting monument to her disobedience. Salt in Scripture is associated with barrenness and desolation (Deuteronomy 29:23; Judges 9:45). She became part of the landscape she could not leave.

Jesus drew the lesson directly. Speaking of the day when the Son of man is revealed, He said, “Remember Lot’s wife,” and added, “Whosoever shall seek to save his life shall lose it” (Luke 17:32–33). Her story shows that being near God’s people, even being led out by angels, does not save someone who will not let go. She had been taken by the hand; she still had to keep walking. Outward association with the faithful is no substitute for a heart surrendered to God (Hebrews 3:12–14).

The verse should not be read with cold satisfaction. A woman who had spent her life in Sodom found it unbearable to leave everything at once, and that is a human sorrow. Yet the warning is meant precisely for those who are close to salvation. What we refuse to release can hold us fast when God calls us forward. Paul’s resolve—“forgetting those things which are behind … I press toward the mark” (Philippians 3:13–14)—is the opposite of her backward gaze.

wordNotes.term: וַתַּבֵּט (wattabbet) — looked
wordNotes.explanation: The same verb נָבַט (nabat) used in the command of verse 17, meaning an intent, purposeful look. Elsewhere it describes the look of faith that brought healing from the brazen serpent and the look toward God that leaves faces radiant. Here it is the look of longing toward a doomed city.

wordNotes.term: נְצִיב מֶלַח (netsiv melaḥ) — a pillar of salt
wordNotes.explanation: נְצִיב (netsiv) is something set up and standing, a post or pillar. Salt marks desolation: Abimelech sowed a conquered city with salt, and Zephaniah warns that Moab will become like Sodom, a place of salt pits and perpetual waste.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham gat up early in the morning to the place where he stood before the LORD:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The scene shifts back to Abraham. “And Abraham gat up early in the morning to the place where he stood before the LORD.” The narrator links this verse to 18:22, where Abraham “stood yet before the LORD” and interceded for Sodom. He returns to the place of prayer, the height from which he and his visitors had looked toward the city (18:16).

Rising early is characteristic of Abraham. He rises early to send Hagar away (21:14) and to set out for Moriah (22:3). In Genesis, early rising signals readiness to meet God’s purposes. This morning Abraham comes without knowing the outcome of his intercession. Had ten righteous been found? Would the LORD spare the city? He returns to the place where he had prayed to see what God had done.

The verse captures something of persevering prayer. Abraham does not forget what he asked, nor does he presume to know the answer. He comes back to the place of meeting. The psalmist describes the same expectancy: “in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up” (Psalm 5:3), and Habakkuk stations himself on the watchtower to see what God will say (Habakkuk 2:1). Faith that has prayed keeps watching for the answer, even when that answer will be hard to bear.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּשְׁכֵּם (wayyashkem) — and gat up early
wordNotes.explanation: שָׁכַם (shakam) means to rise early, usually for purposeful action. It marks Abraham’s prompt obedience on the way to Moriah and Moses’ early rising to build an altar at Sinai.

wordNotes.term: עָמַד אֶת־פְּנֵי יְהוָה (‘amad et-penei YHWH) — stood before the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: To stand before someone is to wait in his presence, ready to serve or to plead. The LORD later names Moses and Samuel as intercessors who “stood before” Him, the same posture Abraham took for Sodom.

verses.bibleText: And he looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the plain, and beheld, and, lo, the smoke of the country went up as the smoke of a furnace.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
From the heights Abraham “looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the plain, and beheld, and, lo, the smoke of the country went up as the smoke of a furnace.” The narrator slows down to show Abraham’s seeing: he looked, he beheld, and lo. What he sees answers his question without a word. Ten righteous were not found. The cities are gone.

Abraham had once surveyed this land when God told him to lift up his eyes and see all of it as promised to his offspring (13:14–15). Now he gazes at part of it reduced to smoke. The “furnace” is a kiln, the kind used for firing pottery or smelting metal, which sends up thick, rolling smoke. The same image describes Sinai when the LORD descended upon it in fire (Exodus 19:18). The furnace smoke over the plain is the trace of God’s holy presence in judgment.

What does Abraham feel? The text does not say. He had pleaded earnestly for the city, and now he sees it destroyed. His silence is fitting. There are moments when faith does not argue but bows before the righteousness of God’s judgments. Abraham had confessed, “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?” (18:25), and now he must rest in that confession.

Revelation borrows this imagery for the fall of Babylon: merchants and kings stand far off and lament when they see the smoke of her burning (Revelation 18:9, 18). The rising smoke testifies that judgment has been carried out. When the fire has done its work, what remains is ash and the vindication of God’s justice.

wordNotes.term: כְּקִיטֹר הַכִּבְשָׁן (keqitor hakkivshan) — as the smoke of a furnace
wordNotes.explanation: קִיטֹר (qitor) is dense smoke; כִּבְשָׁן (kivshan) is a kiln or smelting furnace. Moses took ashes from such a furnace before Pharaoh, and the smoke of Sinai rose “as the smoke of a furnace” when the LORD came down in fire.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when God destroyed the cities of the plain, that God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in the which Lot dwelt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator steps back to summarize: “when God destroyed the cities of the plain, … God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow.” This is the theological heart of the deliverance. Lot was saved because God remembered Abraham.

To “remember” in Scripture is more than recalling a fact. It means to act faithfully on a relationship and a promise. “God remembered Noah” (8:1), and the waters began to recede. God “remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob” (Exodus 2:24), and He began to deliver Israel from Egypt. Here God remembers Abraham’s intercession and his covenant standing, and He brings Lot out. As far as the narrative tells, Abraham never mentioned Lot by name, but his plea for the righteous in Sodom was answered in the rescue of its one righteous household.

The verse is a lesson in intercession. Abraham’s pleading did not save Sodom, because the conditions for sparing it were not met. Yet it was not wasted. God answered in a way Abraham may not have anticipated. James writes, “The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (James 5:16), and this verse shows that prayer can change the outcome for others even when it cannot change the outcome for those who refuse to repent.

The verse also points beyond Abraham. Lot was delivered because of another’s standing before God, not his own. In the gospel, sinners are saved because God honors the covenant sealed in His Son, whose intercession is perfect and unceasing. Christ “ever liveth to make intercession” for those who come to God by Him (Hebrews 7:25). As High Priest in the heavenly sanctuary He pleads for His people, and when the final judgment comes, those who belong to Him will be brought out from the midst of the overthrow as surely as Lot was brought out of Sodom (2 Peter 2:9).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּזְכֹּר אֱלֹהִים (wayyizkor ’elohim) — God remembered
wordNotes.explanation: זָכַר (zakhar) in such statements means that God acts on behalf of someone in faithfulness to His relationship with them. God remembered Noah and the waters receded; He remembered Rachel and opened her womb; He remembered His covenant and moved to deliver Israel.

wordNotes.term: הַהֲפֵכָה (hahafekhah) — the overthrow
wordNotes.explanation: A noun formed from the verb of verse 25, gathering the whole catastrophe into a single word. The prophets use the same root when they speak of God overthrowing Sodom and Gomorrah, holding up the event as the measure of total ruin.

verses.bibleText: And Lot went up out of Zoar, and dwelt in the mountain, and his two daughters with him; for he feared to dwell in Zoar: and he dwelt in a cave, he and his two daughters.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Lot went up out of Zoar, and dwelt in the mountain, and his two daughters with him; for he feared to dwell in Zoar.” The epilogue opens with irony. The town Lot begged for, he now abandons. The mountain he said he could not reach, he now inhabits. The narrator names his motive: fear. Perhaps he sensed that Zoar, a city of the plain, shared the spirit of Sodom and dreaded a similar fate. Whatever the reason, he ends up exactly where God first told him to go (v. 17), but by the road of fear rather than faith.

“And he dwelt in a cave, he and his two daughters.” The contrast with his earlier life is complete. Lot had once been so rich in flocks and herds that the land could not support both him and Abraham (13:5–6). He had a house in Sodom and a seat at its gate. Now he lives in a cave with only two daughters left. His wife is dead, his sons-in-law have perished, his wealth is consumed. The man who chose by sight what looked best ends with almost nothing.

This is where the path of compromise leads. Lot was not a monster; he was a believer who kept choosing comfort and advantage over faithfulness. Jesus asked, “What is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (Matthew 16:26). Lot gained much and lost nearly all, and he was saved only by mercy, “yet so as by fire” (1 Corinthians 3:15). His life stands as a sober picture of what worldliness costs even those whom God rescues.

wordNotes.term: בַּמְּעָרָה (bamme‘arah) — in a cave
wordNotes.explanation: The Hebrew has the article, “the cave,” perhaps a site known to later readers. Caves served as refuges for fugitives, such as the five kings who hid at Makkedah and David hiding from Saul at Adullam. For Lot, once a man of herds and houses, it marks how far he has fallen.

wordNotes.term: כִּי יָרֵא (ki yare’) — for he feared
wordNotes.explanation: The verb יָרֵא (yare’) can describe reverent fear of God or anxious fear of danger. Lot’s fear is the second kind, the fear of man and circumstance that Proverbs calls a snare, in contrast to the confidence of one whose light and salvation is the LORD.

verses.bibleText: And the firstborn said unto the younger, Our father is old, and there is not a man in the earth to come in unto us after the manner of all the earth:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the firstborn said unto the younger, Our father is old, and there is not a man in the earth to come in unto us after the manner of all the earth.” The daughters are not named; they are identified only by birth order, which keeps attention on what they do rather than on who they are. The elder takes the lead.

Her reasoning has two parts. Lot is old, so he will not arrange marriages or father more children; and there is no man to marry them. The second claim is false. Zoar was close by and had been spared. Abraham’s household lived in the hill country to the west. The destruction, however vast, was regional. Perhaps the daughters believed, in their isolation, that their family line was ending, or perhaps they could not imagine marriage outside the circle formed in Sodom. Either way, their reasoning leaves God out entirely.

“After the manner of all the earth” means the ordinary way of marriage and childbearing. They want what is normal, and the desire for children and a future is not wicked. What is wrong is the means they choose. Sarah too had faced the impossibility of childbearing and had been told that nothing is too hard for the LORD (18:14). These women make no appeal to God at all. They decide by their own logic what must be done.

Their words show how thoroughly Sodom had shaped them. They had grown up in a city where moral restraints were mocked, and they had been betrothed to men of that city. Now, under pressure, they reach for a solution the law would later forbid as a grave defilement (Leviticus 18:6–7). Lot had protected their bodies from the mob, but he had not been able to plant God’s principles firmly in their hearts. A parent’s compromise often bears its saddest fruit in the next generation (Proverbs 22:6).

wordNotes.term: הַבְּכִירָה (habbekhirah) — the firstborn
wordNotes.explanation: The feminine form of “firstborn,” used also when Laban insists that the younger daughter may not be given before the firstborn. The narrator identifies the daughters only by birth order, leaving them unnamed throughout the episode.

wordNotes.term: כְּדֶרֶךְ כָּל־הָאָרֶץ (kederekh kol-ha’arets) — after the manner of all the earth
wordNotes.explanation: “The way of all the earth” refers elsewhere to the universal path of death; here “after the manner” of all the earth means the common custom of marriage. A similar idiom describes Sarah as past “the manner of women.”

verses.bibleText: Come, let us make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, that we may preserve seed of our father.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Come, let us make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, that we may preserve seed of our father.” The elder daughter’s plan is deliberate. Her “Come, let us” recalls the builders of Babel (11:3–4), who also devised a human solution to secure their future without God. Here the scheme is darker: to make their father drunk so that he will not know what is being done.

That they need wine shows they knew Lot would refuse if sober. Their plan contains its own verdict; they knew the act was wrong. Scripture later describes strong drink as a mocker and a doorway to shame and folly (Proverbs 20:1; 23:29–35; Habakkuk 2:15), and here wine is the tool by which Lot is degraded. The earlier account of Noah’s drunkenness (9:20–25) had already shown how wine can lead to a father’s dishonor and lasting consequences for the generations that follow.

“That we may preserve seed of our father” states their motive: to keep Lot’s line alive. Concern for posterity ran strong in the ancient world, and it is not hard to see why two women who had lost everything would fear for the future. Yet the language of “seed” is the language of God’s promise to Abraham (12:7; 15:5; 17:7). Abraham and Sarah waited decades for God to give them a seed in His way; Lot’s daughters seize one in theirs. The contrast between promise received by faith and offspring secured by scheming runs throughout Genesis (compare 16:1–4).

The narrative adds no word of condemnation, because the facts speak plainly enough, and the law given later will name this union as forbidden (Leviticus 18:6).

wordNotes.term: נַשְׁקֶה … יַיִן (nashqeh … yayin) — let us make … drink wine
wordNotes.explanation: The causative form of שָׁקָה (shaqah), “to give drink.” Habakkuk pronounces a woe on anyone who gives his neighbor drink to make him drunk in order to look on his nakedness, an almost exact description of this scheme.

wordNotes.term: וּנְחַיֶּה … זָרַע (unḥayyeh … zara‘) — that we may preserve seed
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “that we may keep alive seed.” The same verb and noun appear when God tells Noah to bring animals into the ark “to keep seed alive upon the face of all the earth.” What God secured by His command, Lot’s daughters attempt by their own device.

verses.bibleText: And they made their father drink wine that night: and the firstborn went in, and lay with her father; and he perceived not when she lay down, nor when she arose.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they made their father drink wine that night: and the firstborn went in, and lay with her father; and he perceived not when she lay down, nor when she arose.” The plan is carried out without hesitation. The narration is plain and spare; it reports the facts and moves on, as if the sordidness needs no elaboration.

“He perceived not” uses the verb “know.” The word that marked the mob’s demand (v. 5) and Lot’s offer of daughters who had not “known” a man (v. 8) returns in a final, bitter twist. Lot, who had offered his daughters to be known by the men of Sodom, now does not know what his daughters are doing to him. The irony is deliberate and painful.

Lot’s drunkenness does not erase his responsibility. He allowed himself to be made drunk, and he would allow it again. Isolated, grieving, and passive, he had stopped guarding himself. Hosea warns that wine and new wine take away the heart (Hosea 4:11), and Paul sets drunkenness against being filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18). Self-control is part of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23) and one of the ways God protects the whole person, body and mind together.

In the traditional Hebrew text, scribes placed a dot over one word in this verse, “when she arose,” a mark perhaps reflecting ancient puzzlement over how much Lot truly perceived. Whatever its meaning, the narrative shows a man who no longer governed himself.

wordNotes.term: וְלֹא־יָדַע (welo’-yada‘) — and he perceived not
wordNotes.explanation: The verb יָדַע (yada‘), “know,” here means awareness. Its use recalls the mob’s demand to “know” the guests and Lot’s description of daughters who had not “known” a man. The drunkard in Proverbs likewise says he was struck and did not know it.

wordNotes.term: בְּשִׁכְבָהּ וּבְקוּמָהּ (beshikhbah uvequmah) — when she lay down, nor when she arose
wordNotes.explanation: Lying down and rising up is a common pairing for the whole span of activity. Moses uses it of teaching God’s words at every moment of life, and the psalmist confesses that God knows his downsitting and uprising. Here it measures Lot’s complete unawareness.
