verses.bibleText: And it came to pass on the morrow, that the firstborn said unto the younger, Behold, I lay yesternight with my father: let us make him drink wine this night also; and go thou in, and lie with him, that we may preserve seed of our father.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass on the morrow, that the firstborn said unto the younger, Behold, I lay yesternight with my father: let us make him drink wine this night also.” The elder sister reports what she has done and urges her sister to do the same. There is no sign of remorse or second thought. The first act becomes the pattern for the second.

The repetition is part of the narrator’s point. Sin rarely stays a single act. What is done once becomes easier to do again, and what one person begins draws another in. The elder daughter’s initiative now carries her younger sister with her. The same motive is restated, “that we may preserve seed of our father,” as though saying it again made it more convincing.

The scene is a small illustration of the downward movement Paul describes, where people not only do what is wrong but approve those who practice it (Romans 1:32). Sodom’s influence did not stay in Sodom. It traveled in the hearts of those who escaped and resurfaced in a cave in the hills. Removal from a wicked environment is a mercy, but the mind must also be renewed (Romans 12:2).

wordNotes.term: אֶמֶשׁ (’emesh) — yesternight
wordNotes.explanation: The adverb refers to the previous night. Laban uses it when he tells Jacob that God warned him in a dream the night before. Here it introduces the elder daughter’s matter-of-fact report and her proposal to repeat the act.

verses.bibleText: And they made their father drink wine that night also: and the younger arose, and lay with him; and he perceived not when she lay down, nor when she arose.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they made their father drink wine that night also: and the younger arose, and lay with him; and he perceived not when she lay down, nor when she arose.” The verse repeats verse 33 almost word for word, changing only the daughter. The narrator uses repetition as a mirror: the same scheme, the same drunkenness, the same unknowing father.

Repetition in Hebrew narrative often signals emphasis, and here it underscores how completely passive Lot has become. Throughout the chapter he is acted upon: guests pull him indoors, angels lead him out, and now his daughters make him drunk. The man who once lifted up his eyes and chose for himself (13:10–11) has lost the capacity to choose at all.

The younger daughter follows her sister’s lead, showing how influence works within families for good or ill. Scripture’s wisdom urges companions who lead toward God rather than away from Him (Proverbs 13:20). Yet even in this sad scene God is not absent. He remains Lord of history and will bring His purposes through the descendants of this night, as the book of Ruth will one day show.

wordNotes.term: הַצְּעִירָה (hatstse‘irah) — the younger
wordNotes.explanation: The adjective comes from the root צָעַר (tsa‘ar), “to be small,” the same root behind Lot’s “little one” and the name Zoar. Joseph’s brothers are seated by age, the youngest last, and Jeremiah later speaks of Moab’s little ones crying out.

verses.bibleText: Thus were both the daughters of Lot with child by their father.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Thus were both the daughters of Lot with child by their father.” The summary states the result flatly. The plan succeeded. There is no miracle here, no promise, no word from the LORD. In Abraham’s household, conception comes again and again as God’s gift in answer to promise (18:10; 21:1–2). In Lot’s family it is the product of human scheming.

The narrator’s restraint does not imply approval. Scripture often records events without comment and lets the surrounding story and the law of God interpret them. Israel would hear this account in the light of the commandment forbidding such unions (Leviticus 18:6–7) and would recognize it as the bitter harvest of Lot’s choice to settle in Sodom. Yet God does not abandon the children who are born. He would later give their descendants lands of their own and forbid Israel to seize them (Deuteronomy 2:9, 19). The sins of parents do not place children beyond the reach of God’s care (Ezekiel 18:20).

wordNotes.term: וַתַּהֲרֶיןָ (wattaharena) — were with child
wordNotes.explanation: From הָרָה (harah), “to conceive.” The same verb describes Hagar’s conception by human arrangement and Sarah’s conception at the time God had spoken. The contrast between scheming and promise runs through these chapters.

verses.bibleText: And the firstborn bare a son, and called his name Moab: the same is the father of the Moabites unto this day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the firstborn bare a son, and called his name Moab: the same is the father of the Moabites unto this day.” The elder daughter names her son, and the name sounds like “from father,” recalling his origin. The Greek translation of the Old Testament even adds an explanatory phrase to that effect. The child becomes the ancestor of Moab, the nation east of the Dead Sea that would play a long part in Israel’s history.

“Unto this day” signals that the narrator’s audience knew the Moabites well. Israel met them on the way to Canaan, where Balak king of Moab hired Balaam to curse Israel and the women of Moab drew Israel into idolatry and immorality at Baal-peor (Numbers 22–25). Moab was barred from the congregation of the LORD because it did not meet Israel with bread and water and hired Balaam against them (Deuteronomy 23:3–4). The hostility was religious and political, not merely a matter of ancestry.

Yet the best-loved Moabite in Scripture is Ruth. She left her gods, declared “thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God” (Ruth 1:16), and became the great-grandmother of David and an ancestor of Jesus Christ (Ruth 4:13–17; Matthew 1:5). The line that began in the darkness of a cave was touched by grace. God’s purposes are not limited by human origins, and a people born of Lot’s shame gave the Messiah’s family tree a woman of exemplary faith. The gospel reaches even those whose beginnings are marked by sin.

wordNotes.term: מוֹאָב (Mo’av) — Moab
wordNotes.explanation: The name sounds like מֵאָב (me’av), “from a father,” and the Greek translation adds a phrase explaining it that way. Whatever its original derivation, the narrator lets the sound recall the child’s origin. Ruth the Moabitess later becomes part of the line of David.

wordNotes.term: עַד־הַיּוֹם (‘ad-hayyom) — unto this day
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase links an ancient event to realities familiar to the narrator’s readers, as with the well named Shebah and the sinew Israel does not eat. It shows that Moab was a living neighbor when Genesis was first heard.

verses.bibleText: And the younger, she also bare a son, and called his name Ben-ammi: the same is the father of the children of Ammon unto this day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the younger, she also bare a son, and called his name Ben-ammi: the same is the father of the children of Ammon unto this day.” The name means “son of my people” or “son of my kinsman,” again pointing to the child’s origin within the family. His descendants, the Ammonites, settled northeast of Moab, east of the Jordan, with their chief city at Rabbah, the site of modern Amman.

Ammon, like Moab, became a frequent adversary of Israel. The Ammonites oppressed Israel in the days of Jephthah (Judges 10:7–9), threatened Jabesh-gilead in Saul’s time (1 Samuel 11:1–2), and fought against David (2 Samuel 10:1–6). Their worship of Molech, with its child sacrifice, was especially abhorrent (1 Kings 11:7; Leviticus 18:21). Yet God had given them their land as a possession for Lot’s sake and forbade Israel to take it (Deuteronomy 2:19). Even Lot’s descendants were not forgotten by the God who remembered Abraham.

The chapter ends quietly, with genealogy rather than judgment. Lot fades from the story; Genesis never mentions him again. His legacy is two nations born of a sad night and often hostile to the people of promise. The contrast with Abraham, whose seed would bless all the families of the earth, could hardly be sharper. Yet the prophets foresaw a day when the LORD would bring again the captivity of Moab and of the children of Ammon (Jeremiah 48:47; 49:6). The last word over the families of the earth belongs not to their origins but to the grace of the God who calls them home.

wordNotes.term: בֶּן־עַמִּי (Ben-‘ammi) — Ben-ammi
wordNotes.explanation: “Son of my people.” The noun עַם (‘am) can also mean a paternal kinsman, so the name may hint at the child’s parentage within the family. The Greek translation again adds a short explanation. His descendants are later called בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן (benei ‘ammon), “the children of Ammon.”

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What does it look like for a believer to live inside a culture without that culture coming to live inside him?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: The Judge of all the earth judges sin justly and finally, yet in mercy He draws out those who will leave, saving them for the sake of His covenant rather than their merit.
discussionQuestions: How does the contrast between Abraham’s tent in chapter 18 and Lot’s house in Sodom shape the way we read this chapter?
What do Genesis 19, Ezekiel 16:49–50, and Jude 7 together reveal about the sins of Sodom?
Why did Lot’s warning sound like a joke to his sons-in-law, and what does that suggest about credible witness?
What does verse 16 teach about the relationship between God’s mercy and human hesitation?
How does Jesus use the days of Lot and Lot’s wife to prepare His followers for His return?
commonMisunderstandings: The narrator records Lot’s offer of his daughters without approving it; Scripture never presents that offer as righteous.
Sodom’s sin was neither inhospitality alone nor sexual sin alone; Scripture names violence, pride, neglect of the poor, and sexual perversion together.
The “eternal fire” of Jude 7 is a fire whose results are permanent, not cities that are still burning or people tormented without end.
Lot was not saved because his faith was strong; he was saved by the LORD’s mercy and for Abraham’s sake.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold together the reality of judgment and the urgency of mercy: God’s patience is real, His judgment is final, and His call to leave a doomed world is the voice of a Rescuer.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Let the hands that drew Lot from Sodom take hold of you, and do not look back; follow the Lord fully toward the refuge He provides in Christ.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God will judge the world in righteousness and bring sin to a complete end, but He first sends warning and extends mercy to all who will come out and follow Him.
flow: Sodom’s wickedness rose to heaven as a cry, and God came down to examine it before acting.
Before the fire fell, God sent messengers with a plain warning and a call to leave.
Lot lingered, yet the LORD in mercy took his hand and brought him out.
Lot’s wife left the city in body but not in heart, and she perished on the road to safety.
Christ now calls every person out of a world under judgment into the safety of His saving grace.
simpleIllustrations: A fire warden pounding on doors at night may seem alarmist until the flames crest the ridge; the warning was love all along.
Someone carried out of a burning building is safe only if he keeps moving away from the fire instead of running back for his belongings.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you let the Lord take your hand today and lead you out, without looking back?
cautions: Do not use this chapter to single out one group of sinners while ignoring the pride, greed, and cruelty that Scripture also names in Sodom.
Do not present Sodom’s fire as an ever-burning torment; Scripture describes it as complete and final destruction.
Do not excuse Lot’s offer of his daughters or make light of the abuse this chapter narrates.

reflectionQuestions: Where have I pitched my tent toward Sodom, moving step by step into settings that dull my sense of right and wrong?
Would my warning about eternal things sound credible to my family, or would they think I was joking?
What possessions, relationships, or habits make me linger when God calls me to move?
Is there anything behind me that my heart keeps turning back to look at?
How can I intercede for others as Abraham did, trusting God to answer in His own way?
